utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Wednesday. Let me first greet and wish a good morning to all the people in and around the courtroom. Good morning to you, Mr. Maric. Good morning to all the accused, the Defence counsel, and my renewed wishes for a Happy New Year for Mr. Karnavas who is here with us today for this year 2010. And good morning to you Ms. West, and to your case manager. Including in my greetings all the people assisting us. Today we're going to continue with the cross-examination. Without further ado, you may proceed, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Maric. I'd like to start off from where we left yesterday. When we finished, we were talking about ammunition and the HVO. And specifically I was showing you a comment that General Praljak made during his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can I have Sanction, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And it regarded control of the ammunition. We'll just wait a moment for that comment to come up. Here we go. And in it he was asked generally about ammunition and who was in charge of it, and his answer at line 19, in transcript 24407, is that: "The chief of the artillery of the Main Staff controlled the amount of ammunition used, how much ammunition there was left in the depots." So, sir, my question for you is: did the Main Staff control the amount of ammunition used?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff collected information from lower levels, and thus it did have at its disposal information about the quantity of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And on a more general level, yesterday we also spoke about the different artillery regiments, specifically the rocket regiment. We spoke about the ammunition used -- excuse me, the artillery used in brigades and the battalions and also the operation zone. And on a more general level, in regard to all that testimony, would you say that it's fair to conclude that the Main Staff exerted strong control over the artillery?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff did have control, and I wouldn't be able to call it strong control. It was just control like in any other military.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. If you can't call it strong control but you have compared it to control in any other military, what sort of adjective would you use? Was it competent control? Was it direct control?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That control went from the superior commands to the inferior commands to the extent the brigade can -- had control at its level to the same -- to the same extent the military district had control over its units. Professional organs conveyed information from time to time to professional bodies in the Main Staff. At their briefings, those bodies probably briefed their own superiors in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Just for the record, I believe earlier, I don't have it on my transcript, it's line 6, page 2, when I refer to a transcript that was 44407 - the transcript says 2. So let's talk s little bit more about this control. And I'd like to go to a document. So you have the binder in front of you, and I'm going to give you numbers, and you can turn to them. At the same time on the screen in front of you, you'll also see the documents. The first is P00343. It's the very first one, I think. So, sir, this is the first document in the binder, and it's a document dated July 22nd, 1992, and on top it says "urgent summons for artillery commanders." This is a document issued by General Petkovic and it says: "Artillery commanders or persons in charge of artillery shall report to the main headquarters of the HVO on July 22nd ... to give details on the types, number, and deployment of artillery." Mr. Maric, would you agree with me that this document evidences that the Main Staff, at least in July of 1992, resorted some type of control over the artillery?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't see in this document the area where I was active, and I wouldn't dare to comment upon the rest of the document. In other words, the specific document does not refer to the area where I acted.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric. We're going to go directly to that area now, P03983, P03983. This is a document dated August 6th, 1993, and it's signed by General Tole.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, would you repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, 03983. And perhaps, at least in the beginning, the usher might be able to provide assistance. You have in front of you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got it on the screen, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So this is August 1993, and this is to the south-east command. It's an order, and number 1 says: "I hereby appoint Mijo Jelic, commander of the defence of the town of Mostar. "2. All units in Mostar are placed under his command." And then if you move down to 5, it explicitly says: "The HVO Main Staff is to take over the command of the defence of Mostar." So, sir, come August 1993, not only was the HVO in direct command over the south-east command zone, as we talked about yesterday, but in August of 1993, it directly took over the defence of Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it arises from this document that the Main Staff of the HVO indeed took over the defence of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So when the Main Staff took over the defence of Mostar, you'd agree with me that it also became directly responsible for those weapons controlled by the operational zone of the south-east command in Mostar, specifically Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It arises from this document that the Main Staff took over the command over one part of the front line which up to then was under the command of the operation zone South-east Herzegovina. Only in one part, not in the entire front line of the South-east Herzegovina operation zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric. And as I indicated, we're specifically talking about that one part. We're talking about the city of Mostar. That's where you were located; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my office was in the city of Mostar, and my interest and my zone of activity was across the entire area of the South-east Herzegovina operation zone, which means that the latter was much broader than the zone of the city of Mostar itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And expanding out from the city of Mostar, would you agree, sir, that the Main Staff had control over artillery in all the operational zones?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in operative terms, because in operational zones and in the units that composed the strength of those operational zone, the command over all units was primarily in the hands of the commander of the operational zone where the units were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's look at operator -- excuse me, operative terms -- or, rather, operations. I'd like to go to P01874, 01874. You're going to see it shortly in front of you. And this is an example of artillery in another operational zone. This is the north-west zone. It's a document dated April 13th from General Petkovic. And under number 1, the last paragraph, he writes: "I requested from the Rama Brigade to submit an extraordinary report and ordered them to prepare conditions for artillery activity against mentioned area, but that they should not open fire without our approval." So this is an example where the Main Staff is involved in the operations of an operation -- of a command zone; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection to the way the report is being interpreted. I believe that in these proceedings we have established that this is a collective report from the operation zone. If somebody is talking in the first person singular, it would be the commander of the operational zone, rather than Chief of the Main Staff. The person is mentioned herein, but he's not the author. It says here that this is a report from the South-east Herzegovina operational zone, so when the first person singular is used, then this refers to the part that came from Tomislavgrad. I just want to make sure that everybody understands who is that, me or I, who writes the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has already been addressed. The Trial Chamber is aware that this is a joint report coming from various operation zones and that Petkovic signed this document, which is a compilation of various reports. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, and we'll go back to this. Would you agree with me that this shows that the Main Staff was involved in overseeing or understanding or knowing what the artillery operations were in various operation zones?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, since this refers to the zone in which I had no previous doings, I had no previous information about the nature of the organisation there, about the nature of combat activities that were taking place there, I wouldn't be able to comment upon this document because this doesn't refer to the area or the zone where I perform my duties and where I was active as an officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Maric, we'll talk a little bit more about -- about exactly what your job was. And on Monday you were asked by Ms. Alaburic what -- the question: "As chief of artillery did you have any command capacity?" And your answer at page 35 of the daily transcript was: "The chief of any branch whatsoever does not have any direct connections to any unit nor is he able to command." Sir, I'd like to look at P05361. P05361. This is an August 1993 document. And in it, under number 1, it says, "Decision on action." It says: "In accordance with the orders of the chief of artillery of the Main Staff, deputy Chief of the Main Staff, chief of artillery of the South-eastern Herzegovina operation zones opened fire at the following targets ..." And then it lists some targets. Sir, you were the chief of artillery of the south-east operational zone; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the chief of artillery in the South-east Herzegovina operational zone, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this document says: "In accordance with the orders," you being one of those people, it suggests your order, "they open fire at the following targets, Rastani, Orthodox church," and then it goes on. Do you remember giving such an order, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Madam Prosecutor, this is not an order. This is a report sent from an operational centre of a unit, and it was signed by a lower-ranking officer, the so-called administrative clerk. The chief of artillery could not personally do anything or issue such an order. The chief of artillery could only implement orders received by his -- from his superior commander. What you read in this report does not arise from the fact that the chief of artillery of a branch or at one level had indeed issued an order.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But, sir, were you aware of this? Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I remember those days, and I remember certain activities on the front line in the military district of Mostar -- or, rather, South-east Herzegovina. However, I cannot confirm nor was it possible for a chief of branch to issue an order to any unit whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Not -- notwithstanding, sir, you did indicate if -- you've agreed that, indeed, you were the chief of artillery for the South-eastern Herzegovina operation zone, so can you tell me why at this time in April -- August of 1993 the HVO would be targeting an Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in August 1993, the Orthodox church was nothing but a heap of stones. In some places in the vicinity those stones were used to construct shelters for equipment and manpower. That building had been destroyed long before. The term that the duty operations officer might use and the practice that he might use guided him to mention the general region where military targets were. In military documents, all targets are enumerated. They are assigned numbers. This officer, at his level, did not necessarily have to know the numerical designations of such targets. He was probably only familiar with the region. This report mainly served for logistical purposes and provided an opportunity to monitor the ammunition status at any point in time and its consumption. And this was the purpose of this report. This was an internal unit report which was never sent anywhere, either to a lower or to a higher level. It was primarily and exclusively used by the unit and in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to change subjects, and on Monday you were -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just ask a little question regarding this document. It is signed -- it is signed, I quote, "Gospodin Darko Eric." That strikes me as not normal for a military document. Normally a military officer would sign with his grade. Do you have an explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this gentleman Darko Eric, is an NCO. And that time he had no rank, no rank at all. Only later did he become a non-commissioned officer. And generally he was a desk officer, an administrative person. He -- his qualification was in writing. He couldn't really describe military situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I point out that just in case it causes anybody to raise questions in their heads, that the dates above the signature in the report compiled the 24th September, 1994, that's just an error. The original says 1993. Just in case it set any alarm bells ringing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Colonel, I must tell you that when I saw this document I see that the target here is an Orthodox church. I initially felt that this document might be a Prosecution document. And it's stated that only the stones were left, but I think there's something missing for any reasonable trier of fact. According to you, when was this church actually destroyed, on what date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't recall the date, but it was much earlier during the conflicts with the Army of Republika Srpska and the Yugoslav People's Army, sometime in the middle of 1992, that is to say perhaps over a year before this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document could in effect be construed in the way you are saying it, because the document states a number of places and not specific targets. What is the place -- where was this Orthodox church located? Thirteen places are mentioned here. Where was this church actually?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: This could be incriminating evidence, instead of Prosecution evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Orthodox church is located to the east of Mostar, some hundred metres above the M17 road connecting Konjic, Jablanica, Mostar, Metkovic, and Neum, in an unpopulated area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it around Rastani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It's about 3 kilometres away from Rastani, perhaps 4. East of Mostar, on an elevation overlooking the M17 road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand correctly, the soldiers of the opposing party picked up the stones to build bunkers; is that right? So you felt that it was necessary to fire shots on this location to prevent them from building any bunkers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the nearer and more distant environs of that church, there are natural features that with minor use of these rocks provided adequate shelter from the firing of the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Your Honour. With your leave, I just want to draw your attention to something illogical that is obviously an error in the original document, and thus in the translation as well. If we look at the date of this document, we'll see it's the 24th of August; and if we look at the last line in the document, it says the report was done for the day of 24 September. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, on Monday you were asked about the procurement of artillery, and the question was: "Tell us briefly, Mr. Maric, how did you procure artillery weapons?" And your answer on daily transcript 37 was: "We started in the end of 1991 acquiring a very small number of artillery weapons. And in the beginning of 1992, we acquired a larger number from several sources. Part of the artillery weapons procured in my area came from Travnik, because Travnik had certain bases. I don't know exactly what sources in Travnik, but I know that we required some more from Travnik. I know we required more from Croatia because there were still no public borders at the time." Mr. Maric, what is the time-frame for your acquisition of weapons from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely that period, the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And did you get artillery from Croatia any time later than the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, Madam Prosecutor, I as technical professional officer had the duty to draw up the assignment -- to describe the assignment to my superior and state our requirements in keeping with the situation on the front line. By that time the logistics was already in place as a separate department, and it was their job to deal with procurement. I did not have to know when and from where those weapons were required. My job was, one, to use the existing personnel and the weapons we had to create a good team, a good unit that would meet the requirements in combat in keeping with the rules of fire and other rules that had existed first in the JNA and that we had taken over and used in that first period.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Procurement didn't go through me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. You just said procurement didn't go through you, but when we look at what you said on Monday, it appears that you had detailed knowledge in regard to procurement. So I'd like to look at P03071. P03071. This is a July 1993 -- July 1st, 1993 order -- sorry, not order. It looks to be a letter from Bruno Stojic. And it is to an individual named Rojs, R-o-j-s. It's entitled request for artillery ammunition. And it says: "Since we were left with no artillery ammunition for 203-millimetre howitzers and 152-millimetre howitzers, please deliver to us whatever quantity may be possible." Mr. Maric, you're distancing yourself from procurement, but would you agree with me that at least in July of 1993 there appears to be, from this document, artillery coming from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one remark. It's not weapons, it's ammunition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to see the date, but if I can rely on my memory, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had several weapons of this calibre, and at meetings with my colleagues from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they frequently voiced requests to use my connections and the logistics of the HVO to procure these things for them. I remember clearly that at one co-ordination meeting I asked a logistics officer from Mostar, from HVO Mostar, to try to get this for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, we did not succeed. In the military district at that time, we did not have these assets. Once I tried to serve as intermediary to get this ammunition for the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric. You can't see it on the screen, but there's a third page attached to this; it's a fact sheet, and that's where I got the date. Now you've just given us information regarding the BiH Army voice request to you to get -- I'll use your connections and logistics at the HVO to procure these things for them. But assuming that July 1, 1993, is the correct date of this document, you'll agree with me that can't be -- this cannot be an example of that; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case I tried to intercede not in this case but in a different one. I have no comment on this. This is the first time I hear of this request.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, subject -- excuse me, subsequent to July 1993, did you ever hear about the HVO procuring more weapons from Croatia after July of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such information because, I repeat, particularly in the period in mid-1993, my duties and the situation on the front line required me to deal solely with the use of assets in the military district of Mostar. That was a time when the logistics of the HVO had already grown into a respectable organisation that made acquisitions in a way that I was not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric, but if you forgive me, I'm going to press you a little bit more on this. Because on Monday when you were asked this question from Ms. Alaburic, you gave a very detailed answer in regard to how the HVO procured weapons. I'd like you to look at P05562. This is an October 1993 document from Mr. Stojic. P05562. Again this is to Croatia. In the second paragraph it says: "In agreement with Bruno Stojic, defence minister ... Mr. Santic, president of the Vitez HVO, the MTS is to be transported to the Grude logistics base. "We therefore kindly ask you to transport the following MTS ..." And it lists some MTS. Sir, you would agree with me this document would suggest that as far into 1993, October 1993, the HVO was still getting, in this case, MTS from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am really sorry. I have to object to this question. From the first sentence it is quite obvious whose assets these are. They are assets from Croatia, but I would appreciate it if --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Thank you. [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would appreciate it if the witness were allowed to read all of the document. The first sentence makes it clear whose assets these are, and I don't think the question of the Prosecutor is entirely in keeping with the context of the document. Let the witness read the document, and if he has any knowledge he can impart it. I believe this question could mislead the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer, Your Honour, regarding this document is that I know nothing about it. As to whether it is authentic and whether this was possible, I don't know, but I had nothing to do with this kind of task, nor could I know anything about it. With Mr. Bruno Stojic I had only one contact, in the beginning of August. And throughout the war all my work was in the organisation of artillery, and my sole responsibility was towards my superior commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, it's been your testimony that in 1993 there were no offensive actions taken by the HVO, and on Monday daily transcript 35, the question was: "If we set aside the operation Bura, Storm, that was executed in 1992, were the activities of the HVO predominantly defensive or offensive at that time?" And your answer a witness: "Our activities at the time were exclusively defensive." So just to be clear, is it your testimony that your actions -- HVO actions in 1993 were exclusively defensive as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again I have to object to this question, because the reference to the direct examination is not complete. In direct examination we discussed planned offensive actions, which I believe is very important, not offensive actions that would have defence significance, and so the purpose of recovering the territory that had been lost shortly before. So the discussion was about planned offensive actions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer? Perhaps you've found it in the transcript when I said that we mainly dealt with defence and organised defence. You will probably find as well the place where I said I was personally involved and helped with the organisation and planning for the Operation Tempest. So it is true I participated in Operation Tempest by organising and planning in keeping with my duties as chief of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's look specifically at April of 1993 in regard to HVO activity. Specifically look at P01868. P01868. This is an April 14th document. At the top it says - you have it in front of you now: "As per order of the head of the defence department, head of the department of interior, and OZ commander, we herewith present our joint plan for intensified control over the town of Mostar." And then the paragraph is entitled "task." And it says: "Due to the increasingly complex security situation, which as a result of the conflict between the BiH and the HVO in Konjic, all police units and civilian -- and civilian police are to be immediately and not later than 14 April ... at 2200 hours put on active alert, while the 2nd, 3rd, and 5th battalions, and potentially the 4th, of 2nd Brigade are to be put on increased alert, carry out blockade of all entry points, intensify control in the town of Mostar, and cover all important crossroads ... the snipers as a precaution measure, and intensify patrol between 600 and 2200 hours." Sir, April 1993, this was the period of time when you were in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you remember these things happening?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. This is a document from the military police. This is a document from the military police; it does not relate to the army in the operation zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honours, this witness can testify to this because he was in Mostar in April 1993. And my question was, "Do you remember this happening?" As a layperson in Mostar he can answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only reacted when the question was asked, "Do you remember these things happening?" because it relates to the actions of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, the witness and Colonel sitting before us is an intelligent man. He is able to realise that himself without a lawyer intervening. And then it carries much more weight when he says it. It carries more weight than if you say it. Colonel, you have a document in front of you. Who does this document concern, the military police, the army, the civilian police? Are you concerned in any way by this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document does not relate to me, and could I not comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Maric, I'm not asking you to comment on it from an artillery standpoint. But in April of 1993, you were a resident of Mostar. So my question: As a resident, as a person who lived in that city, did you see any activity that would suggest a plan by the HVO for intensified control over the town of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is precisely why I objected. How can we talk about this as a plan of the HVO to control the city of Mostar? This relates mainly to my client General Petkovic who was in charge of the Main Staff at the time. And this document is issued by the military police, an institution that has nothing to do with the Main Staff. That is the point of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to say only the following, that if you have a look at page 1, and in the second part of page 1 under "Combat equipment," here we find that, and I quote: "In addition to regular armament at the disposal of the above-mentioned units, the following is to be provided: "Artillery pieces," so-and-so, "armoured combat vehicle and Bofors anti-aircraft gun," and then, "additional equipment," probably equipment, with snipers, hand-held rocket launchers, and other grenades. So I believe that this very part of that plan for intensified control over the town of Mostar -- city, as it has it in its title, has certain relevance to the artillery actions. So I believe that the witness is able and hopefully ready to make comments on this issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we wish to discuss this document in that way, then I believe the witness should be allowed enough time to read the entire document rather than relying on what he can see on the screen, just the first page without any header, and he hasn't been given time to see who created the document. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] May I just say briefly since military police is mentioned. One can see when one reads the whole document it was not issued by the department of the military police by -- but by a person who is within the military police but on behalf of a group. A special separate group was created but not headed by Mr. Coric, who is not mentioned in this document, by the way, either as a recipient or in any other way by name as a person involved in this action, and we can see who was involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be fair, I have to say one more thing. I agree with what my colleague says, but my inference that it was a document of the military police is based on the seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I was about to say something. Judge Prandler mentioned what I was about to say. You don't know this document because clearly it comes from people who are working for the military police, 3rd Battalion, 1st Company, and so on. I had noted that Mr. Coric is not the recipient of this document, but I had noted, like my fellow Judge Prandler, that these people were being equipped with artillery pieces, and I therefore wondered whether the colonel who is sitting before us knew that the military police could be equipped with artillery pieces, and did he play any role in the -- the providing of this equipment? Maybe the equipment came from elsewhere, maybe not. And we felt, both I and my fellow Judge, that you might be able to tell us something about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the chief of artillery in the military district of Mostar had the responsibility to worry only about the artillery under the direct command of the operations zone Mostar. That means that any other units existing outside the command of the operation zone Mostar and do not form part of its organisation are not subject to the direction of the chief of artillery. He does not have to take care of their replenishment, including assets that are referred to as artillery. But I have to say, to be precise, that these are 60-millimetre calibres which are deployed in assault units as regular infantry weapons. However, according to the characteristics they are similar to artillery weapons, and that word "artillery" was sometimes used even when it was not quite correct to use it. I have another remark. I have only parts of the document on the left, on the right. Therefore, I'm missing parts of the sentences here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P01868. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, if we look at the -- you can look at the B/C/S page 2. You'll also note this was copied to the Main Staff and the OZ commander. So I'm going to repeat my question which is in April of 1993, were you aware of this plan for intensified control over the town of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Madam Usher, if you could please assist. P01928.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is an order from one of the brigade commanders in your operational zone, and it says: "Due to the current situation in the area of responsibility of the 1st Brigade ... I hereby issue the following order: "The 1st, 2nd, and 3rd battalions of the 1st Brigade of the HVO are to prepare one company each. These companies, composed of Croats only, should go on full alert ..." Mr. Maric, do you have any idea as to why on April 17th Colonel Obradovic would be preparing Croat-only companies?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer why the document was issued in this form.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P01998, P01998. This is a document from April of 1993, and it talks about highest level of combat readiness. Sir, yesterday you were asked a question about combat readiness as well, and it's at page 15 of the daily. Question yesterday was: "Mr. Maric, is there a difference between an order to raise combat readiness and an order to launch a certain combat operation?" And your answer was: "An order to raise combat readiness means that all the elements of a unit should be raised to such a level of preparedness that they can be used should that become necessary." So, Mr. Maric, my first question to you is: would you agree with me that an order for combat readiness shows that a military organisation is planning an operation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's look specifically at this one: P01998, April 20th. It's a Lasic order. "For the aim of achieving the highest level of combat readiness and due to the escalation of enemy attacks, I hereby issue the following order." And then it's 1 through 11. And these -- they appear to be a positioning of certain artillery, certain crews. And then number 11 says the deadline for implementation of this order is 24 hours. Sir, do you remember this order from April 20th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And would you agree, then, that south-east operational zone in Mostar was preparing itself for the highest level of combat readiness?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, April the 20th, 1993, was the day when the intelligence services of the HVO informed the OZ command about the order which contained the intent of the BiH Army to organise themselves and raise their combat preparedness, as well as the objectives that pointed to the fact that in the shortest possible time the BH Army in the territories that had been defended by the OZ command would carry out offensive actions. In keeping with that, the minimum duty of a commander was to analyse that intelligence and to issue a set of instructions to his units accordingly, instructions or orders. That's how I interpret the content of this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Maric, you would agree with me, then, by April 20th, or at least on the deadline of this, 24 hours, the next day, that the south-east command HVO then was ready for a combat operation.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Units in the south-east OZ were ready for combat from the moment they had been established; that's as far as the units were concerned. They were always ready to defend the front line, and this order was just another reminder to the units on the front line to be ready for possible attacks launched by the BiH Army --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric --

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that was only and exclusively with the purpose of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Colonel. You know we're working in three languages: your language, the Prosecutor's language, and French, because eventually the judgement will be issued in French. Earlier on the Prosecutor asked you whether this document showed you were combat-ready, and you answered, but there is a nuance, because when you say to be combat-ready, you can be combat ready in responding to an enemy attack, or you can be combat-ready whilst sort of starting combat yourself, an attack yourself. So there are differences used in all these new concepts. And in my language every word has a meaning, and we really have to mince our words. When the Prosecutor asked you whether you were combat ready, that meant that you were the attacker in that case. Can you grasp the difference there is? So back then what did this document mean exactly in military terms? Did it mean that you were going to attack, or alternatively that you were positioning yourselves and that you would respond to an attack if any? So what does this have as a meaning in military terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that yesterday in the course of my testimony I already answered a similar question. If the combat readiness of a unit is increased or in terms of defence, that means that some of the troops should be in the trenches, some of them should be resting. However, those who are active should be as ready and alert as possible. At the moment when an attack is being prepared, I said it already yesterday, it takes a period of at least several days to prepare combat documents which are an integral part of the operation and are used to carry that operation out. And based on such documents, the success or failure of the operation is evaluated post event. What this is about is raising combat readiness in keeping with the intelligence about the offensive activities of the enemy, to prepare the unit for successful defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can offer this to be clear in everybody's minds, whether it be the Prosecutor's side or the Defence's side or the Judges. If I take the instance of the crew under item 5, which is to be positioned in bunker 2 in Hum, is there with the equipment as described, but does nothing. He's going to wait in case there is an offensive action for the plan that is being prepared to be put into action, which is not the case, but it's there positioned in bunker number 2. And he's being -- if he's being fired on, he's going to respond. Is that the way it should work in military terms? Because, you see, we're not from the army; we're not military men, and we have to understand this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely so. A soldier in his position has to be prepared to engage at any moment should his position come under attack. And you, Your Honour, show that you understand the situation well. I believe that you said that you had been an artillery man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you see, but I'm a Judge, and I have to be modest in my knowledge. That's why I lend a listening ear to each and every one. Please continue, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P11162, P11162. This is May 3rd, 1993. It's towards the back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Mindua.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Ms. West. I just -- I had this question I wanted to speak -- to express for a long time, but I was reluctant disturbing the course of your cross-examination, but since the ball in -- is in the Judges' court, I'll ask my question now. Let's go back in time, Witness, regarding the document that Ms. West has just submitted to you, P01928. This was an order, P01928, an order dated 17th of April, 1993. In the order, under paragraph 1, it was said that companies had to be made ready, and they were all to be composed of Croats only. Have you found this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yesterday during examination-in-chief, we examined document 4D1225. It may not be necessary to look at it again. I'm going to sum it up for you. So it was document 4D1225. It mentions mobilisation of a certain number of Muslim soldiers because they had not reported to their respective units. The interesting thing about this is that when we discussed the issue, you said that in June 1993, the Muslim soldiers who wanted to remain within the HVO were allowed to do so. So they could stay within the HVO. So that's why I was a little at a loss before when I saw that in document 1928 mention was made of companies that were to be made up of Croats only. Do you have an explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I did not have an explanation for this. At that time in the units under my control, the numbers of Bosniaks and Muslims equaled the numbers from six months before that. As far as I'm concerned, I don't have an explanation for this. I suppose that this was due to some other reasons. I didn't have any reason at the time to suggest that anybody in the artillery should do the same. Mr. Obradovic is OZ, and he was the one who drafted the document, was quite large. The regions and neighbourhoods were segregated in ethnic terms. At the beginning of my first day of my testimony I said that all the units had been riddled with their old habits by religious and ethnic customs and habits, and that was not forbidden. Sometimes for very highly humanitarian reasons things could happen at the time which are nowadays being interpreted in very negative -- in very negative terms. It's very hard to describe everything that was going on, on just one page. There was some habits that existed in the units at the time. The army was not well organised. The state was still young. At that time, it was allowed for people to group around ethnic affiliations or religious beliefs, because at the time everybody in the unit was allowed to have their religious affiliations and beliefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P11162, which is at the back of the binder, the very end. 11162. It's going to be on the screen shortly. This is May 3rd, 1993. This is a letter from Petkovic and commander -- one more.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Madam Usher, may we ask for assistance, please. There you go.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May 3rd, Stojcic, Marko Stojcic and Petkovic. And it's addressed to the head of artillery zones South-east Herzegovina. That would be you; correct? "Urgently send me the number of weapons and ammunition in your zones of responsibility." Mr. Maric, do you know why they wanted this information?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in the HVO we had continuous obligation to send reports about the status of artillery pieces, ammunition, and other materiel and technical equipment, and we did it as required and as necessary. We also reported about technical inspections and all the other activities that were carried out in the artillery. We sent those reports to our superior along the professional lines. Since this is a report-like document, my superior Marko Stojcic do not sign it himself but, rather, requested approval or somebody to be his cosignatory, and it was Milivoj Petkovic, chief, but somebody signed on his behalf. In other words, this order was part of the correspondence that existed between the superior-inferior professional bodies or between a higher-ranking and a lower-ranking unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric. And indeed at the end of the day yesterday and the beginning of today we spoke about this issue of recording; however, this document, would you agree, appears to be a bit unusual in that it starts with: "Urgently send me the number of weapons and amounts of ammunition in your zones of responsibility!" So I will ask you again, my question is: do you know why they wanted this information so urgently?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I've just said it, the BH Army still has a lot of shortcomings. I have personally witnessed that, and I've personally witnessed of the shortcomings that existed at that time. It did happen that officers in other zones did not submit timely reports as I did. I tried to do it in the timeliest possible fashion. So they didn't submit professional reports in a timely fashion --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and this was requested based on the order that was signed by an officer from the Main Staff who, in my view, was much lower rank -- ranked than the chief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please, Witness. This is not a neutral document, because it can be read in at least two ways, and I'm going to state them for you. The first way or angle is that within the HVO there may be statistics, and then every month you have to know in each operation zone how many ammunitions and equipment there is. That could be every 30th or 31st of the month. And then a lower-ranking officer discovered on the 3rd May that he did not have this statistical information at his disposal. Therefore, there was a reminder requesting the information to be sent, which would account for the exclamation mark and the mention saying "Urgent." That could be one reason. The other reason could be that this was on the 3rd of May, six days before the 9th of May. And the Prosecution case is that the HVO attacked on the 9th of May. And as part of the plan that I haven't seen so far, that I don't have in front of me, the attack was organised. But before it was organised one had to check what was the status in terms of materiel, weapons, and ammunition. So this is this urgent request. So there are two possibilities. There may be a third one, I don't know. But what is, in your view, the reason why it is urgently requested from you to have information, statistical information as to ammunition and this on the 3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: An observation on the transcript. On page 29, line 5, you are reported as having said: "The BH Army still has a lot of shortcomings." In the context, I suppose that you wanted to speak about the HVO here. No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. Your Honours, I'm talking about the present day, about the present situation in the BiH Army, because I am very much interested in that. Some of the officers quoted here, even the officer mentioned in this document is the third or fourth ranking officer in the current army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which I don't think is of little relevance. He is one of the ten most prominent officers in the BiH Army as things stand today. And in order to respond to the Honourable Judge's question about the time, this is just one such order. I'm sure that before that date and after that date, there are -- there were at least a dozen similar orders. Why is that? It happened that certain officers for objective or subjective reasons did not send timely responses to certain queries from their superior commands or from their superior professional bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps -- because I -- I may be wrong, of course. Not the first, neither the last time. I thought that we were talking about the document P11162. Perhaps that is an error. That document is signed by Mr. Petkovic and one Marko Stojcic, who is commander of the artillery. The witness -- Mr. Maric, you have been speaking of a low-ranking officer. I -- I don't understand. And I don't understand what this says about the organisation of the BH Army. So I would like to be clear on this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about the presentation situation in the organisation of the BiH Army, and I wanted to tell you that it is far from ideal, even 15 years on. It could not have been expected to be ideal at the time when this order was issued with a view to collecting reports on the artillery in this OZ. This was my way to illustrate the situation and to tell you that it was no -- not a surprise if somebody was late with sending their reports, and it was a way to alert them to their omission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you had added something else. You looked at the signatures, just as I did, and you observed that the signatory was not Colonel Petkovic and was not Marko Stojcic either, because you noted, just as I did, that it was on behalf of. So those who signed must have been lower-ranking officers, those officers who did not have the same rank as Stojcic or Petkovic. Is that what you meant? Because in your language, where it's bit like mine, you know, we speak fast, and there is some nuance that may escape us. Is that what you meant then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. That's what I meant. Marko Stojcic's signature and Petkovic's signature, actually, these are not their signatures. Marko Stojcic's was signed by the advisor for artillery, and Petkovic's signature -- actually, it was signed on his behalf by somebody else. However, us, who were familiar with the organisation at the time, when we read such orders and when we see these signatures, if I may say so, we give somewhat less significance to such documents than we do to the documents that were personally signed by the persons whose names are typed on such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, following up on your way to analyse the possible significance of this document, and I totally agree that the two alternatives that you presented are absolutely possible, maybe you should ask the witness who the document was addressed to. If we are able to identify the addressee and the region, we may be able to either establish or lose the connection with the region of Mostar where the present witness was active. Maybe you should ask him about the addressees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is the addressee of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the addressees were chiefs of artillery in the OZ South-east Herzegovina, and the other two int he HVO. What I'm saying is that those were not bodies that could have proceeded to act. The only thing they could do was to draft reports or do something similar as prescribed by the duties of chiefs of artillery. They could not issue any orders. They could only compile statistical database on this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a correction in the transcript about a line or two lines are missing. The witness said OZ South-east Herzegovina, and the other two OZs. What is missing is the fact that the figure two relates to OZs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The operational zones for those people who are interested in that are listed in the document. All you need to do is read the document. It's time for the break now. It's already 35 minutes past 10.00. I should like to remind Ms. West that she will have an hour and a half left. We shall have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mrs. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're going to briefly go back to P11162. This is the urgent letter from Petkovic and Stojcic. And I don't have your testimony in front of me, but I think we'll all remember that in answer to a question you propose that a possible explanation for the urgency tone in this letter was because some OZs had been tardy in their reports and that perhaps this was an urgent reminder to get them to send their reports. Now, sir, I'm going to ask you again. Let's put that possible explanation aside and ask for your specific memory, because this document was sent to you, specifically to you. Do you know why they wanted this information so urgently?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, as in any other time when something similar was required by the superior command or by the superior professional organ, that information was always sent in this form. Sometimes urgently, sometimes less speedily. It depended mostly on the person drawing this up or the organ concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Madam Usher, I think the witness is going to need some help with these documents. He seems not to be able to get through the binder very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P02209. May 6, 1993. This is an order from Petkovic to the Ludvig Pavlovic unit, to Dragan Curcic, who was a witness here, to him personally. It was on May 6th, and says: "Due to the situation in the Konjic and Jablanica sectors, and with the aim of providing assistance at the defence lines, I hereby order. "1. Increase unit combat readiness to the highest level." So again, Mr. Maric, we see this language "combat readiness to the highest level." Sir, do you agree with me that this could be one of those occasions outside the norm where General Petkovic's asking that the units be on extra alert, more intensive alert, not just the normal alert that you spoke about earlier?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, from the very establishment of HVO units in 1992, I emphasised that there were, along territorial, family, and similar principles, frequent allowances. Depending on the situation on the ground, it was necessary for the competent superior commander, from time to time, to send an officer out from the command or to send document ordering a higher level of alert and readiness, because we know that there was a service in every command that a monitored some actions that had the potential to disrupt the existing degree of mobility and readiness of a unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that troops were being sent to Jablanica; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But generally you understand that the road from Jablanica running south -- ran south from Jablanica to Mostar; correct? We talked about this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This was a road which could be used as a route by which the ABiH could supply their troops in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BH Army, until 9th of May, 1993, was fully able to use the M17 road from south towards Jablanica, Konjic, and on to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now let's look at the time after May 9th. You would agree with me that if the HVO was able to control this road from Jablanica, the HVO could limit the amount of supplies the ABiH could bring into Mostar from the north; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean this order, it doesn't say anywhere that this unit is going to Jablanica or along which route.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, Mr. Maric, that wasn't my question. Let me ask you in a different way. Subsequent to May 9th, in the summer of 1993, would you agree with me generally that if the HVO was able to control the road that ran from Jablanica to Mostar, it would limit the amount of supplies the ABiH could bring into Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period the HVO did not control that road.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, what is your opinion as to who started the war between the HVO and the ABiH on May 9th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my deep conviction, Your Honours, that the conflict between the BH Army and the HVO on the 9th of May was started and provoked by extremist factions in the BH Army, which at that time had a predominant role in decision-making within the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Madam Usher, if you can give us some assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P02215. This is a document from the 1st Brigade, 7 May 1993. 2215. This is from -- an order from Colonel Obradovic. And number 1, he says: "All unit commanders and complete commands are to go to their command posts immediately." Number 4: "The 3rd Battalion in co-operation with the police is to reinforce its check-points and not to allow any Muslims through. "5. Immediately mobilise all Croats in the companies which are on leave." I'm going to skip - you have the B/C/S in front of you - to 7. Makes a number of points. One of them is the full readiness, the Medical Corps. "10. Chief of the anti-aircraft defence is to immediately ensure ..." and then it speaks about certain guns. And then number 11 says: "The chief of artillery shall ensure the full readiness of his units reconnoiter with the following positions as agreed upon." And you go to number 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, it says: "All chiefs shall establish contact with their vertical superiors and draw up plans and maps." Mr. Maric, were you aware of this order?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall it. I don't remember that it came to my desk.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So May 7th of 19 -- 1993, this is a 1st Brigade order. But under 12 it says: "All chiefs shall establish contact with their vertical superiors and draw up plans." And, sir, you were not -- you were the assistant commander of artillery to the OZ, to the south-east command, so you would have been one of those vertical superiors to this brigade when it came to the issue of artillery; right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. This order was sent to the structures of command and control within this unit. And as far as I know, and I believe I remember well, I did not receive any request or information. And this can be associated, perhaps, with the previous document, which means that somebody must have or should have informed me if urgent reaction was needed. I don't know of this order. No documents were sent to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, you earlier testified that you believe on May 9th that event was started by extremist factions in the BH Army. I'm going to -- we're going to move to other peoples and organisations' opinion about the same event and talk about that. I'd like to go to P02241, P02241.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It's under seal, Your Honour. May we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The next document can be in open session, but it cannot be broadcast. This is P02237. P02237. This is an ECMM report dated May 9th. 2237.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to read a couple parts of this, and ask you a question. Under number 1, second paragraph: "After checking by CC Grude, it is now confirmed that fighting using, in particular, mortars, started this morning at 0500 hours with clear HVO attacks on BiH positions inside of the town. Attacks were simultaneously conducted on BiH forces north of Mostar halfway to Jablanica, in Dreznica, which is quite the last stronghold of BiH in the centre of a completely HVO-controlled road to Jablanica." And if you go under number 3, "Comments" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Number 3, "Comments." "If a large-scale offensive is sustained by the HVO in Mostar -- if a large-scale offensive is sustained by the HVO in Mostar and its large area, as it seems to be the case, it will confirm quite definitely its plans to take control asap of all Western Herzegovina, despite all promises made previously." Sir, my question for you is whether you were aware of any such plans?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was never aware of such plans. The term "Western Herzegovina" covers an area from the river of Neretva to the west, all the way to the border of Croatia. And it is known that from the 9th of May the line was set up deep in Mostar and that deep in Mostar there was a territory under the control of the BiH Army, which proves that --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Moric, excuse me. This is one of those occasions that I was looking for an answer that was either a yes or no or I don't know. So I'll ask you another question, and we'll try to see if you can respond in that way. P01866. P01866. April 13th. This is entitled "Record," from Brigadier Lasic. April 13th. It says: "Record of the South-eastern Herzegovina operation zone commander's meeting with the commanders of the immediately subordinated units and assistant commanders." Sir, you were an assistant commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was not assistant commander. I was a professional member of the command of the Eastern Herzegovina OZ. There is a big difference and a substantial difference there. I was a professional member of the command. That's what I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is a record of a meeting, and this is Lasic's record of it. And under number 2, if you go to the bottom, it says: "The responsible military structures (Defence Office and Main Staff) are expected to define and state in a clearer way their attitude concerning those who are stalling the implementation of the provinces in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They are also expected to point out the right way to fight in order to prevent what happened in Prozor, Konjic, Kljuic from happening in other municipalities of the Neretva valley." So I want to focus here on the language "implementation of the provinces of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna." Sir, would you agree with me that it was the HVO plan to take over the provinces in the area of Herceg-Bosna for the benefit of the Croats who live there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the translation here refers to the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and I don't see it in the document -- or, rather, in the interpretation I heard a reference being made to the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, whereas this doesn't exist in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, why don't you read out number 2 in your language.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my language it reads, "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna," which is nothing like the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Quite the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, sir. Mr. Maric, I want you to read all of paragraph 2 -- or number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read out the paragraph in your language, and your words will be translated by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The responsible military structure, the Defence Department, and the Main Staff are requested to take a more clear stance towards those who are preventing the implementation of provinces in keeping with Vance-Owen plan within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that they should emphasise how the fighting is being conducted, how it should be conducted in order to prevent what happened to Prozor -- in order to prevent what happened to Prozor, Konjic, and Jablanica from happening in other parts of the Neretva valley. Lastly, they are expected to clarify whether there are any bodies and which ones exactly that co-ordinate these issues at the level of the HZ HB."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West then asked the witness to read out this text because I saw the English version, and I read "The Croatian republic." So, indeed, this could be a considerable incriminating piece of evidence. But in the original it's not said "Republic" but "Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." Well, not quite the same thing. This is not the first time that supposedly incriminating documents have been translated in a doubtful way. This is really very kind on my part.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I appreciate that. I hope nobody was prevented from understanding the full implication of this document, but it is dated April 1993, and it's clear that that's not when the republic existed, so I think we all understand it to be the community. But we'll go right to Mr. Maric's words as they were translated. And he says that: "Take a more clear stance towards those who are preventing the implementation of provinces in keeping with the Vance-Owen Plan within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, sir, would you agree with --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Microphone not activated] -- say something. Just a second. [Interpretation] I apologise for the interruption from what Madam Prosecutor replied to Judge Antonetti's remark, it seems that she doesn't see a problem with the translation of this document. I totally agree with His Honour Judge Antonetti about the difference being substantial. I would kindly request the Trial Chamber to order the Prosecution to have the document translated properly and that the existing translation be replaced in e-court by a new correct translation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, anyway, it's now on record because this has been interpreted or translated by the interpreters here in the courtroom, and it has been mentioned that it is not the republic, but the community. I think that's settled. But there's a difference, Ms. West, between the HZ HB and the HR HB. Do you agree with that or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do agree with that. My only point is it's now corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So I'll go back to my question which is at line 13, page 52. Would you agree with me that it was the HVO plan to take over the provinces in the area of Herceg-Bosna for the benefit of the Croats who lived there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, at that time what was offered was a plan drafted by the highest authorities who dealt with the issues of the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric excuse me --

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan that was in place was considered --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My apologies again, but this about the fourth time I've asked that. When I ask you a question where the appropriate response is yes, no, or I don't know, I would expect that answer. So again my question is: would you agree with me that if the HVO plan to take over the provinces in the area of Herceg-Bosna was for the benefit of the Croats who lived there. If the answer is no, say no. If it's I don't know, say I don't know.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with you that the HVO intended to take those provinces which were inhabited by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, yesterday you were asked questions by Judge Antonetti in regard to the Old Bridge, and one at transcript 4823 -- yep?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move on to the Old Bridge, let us return to the previous document. Madam Prosecutor, this is a meeting of the 13th April that you tie up with the 9th May events. You're looking for a motive behind the events of the 9th May. And she said to you, Look at this meeting mentioned in this. So she's making a connection between this and the 9th of May. But I first note that the commander of the 1st Brigade, the Knez Domagoj Brigade, was absent from the meeting. That's somewhat curious to me. Because if this 13th April meeting should prepare what is about to happen on the 9th May, number one officer, Obradovic, why is he not at the meeting? That's my first remark. Second observation, under paragraph 2 that Ms. West asked you to read out, which you did and it's now recorded in the transcript, my impression is that Miljan Koljesic [sic] is trying to get together the military and the civilians around these politically orientated problems, reminding what happened in Prozor, Konjic, and Kljuic, and in other municipalities of the Neretva valley, expecting these people to clarify all this and expecting some kind of co-ordination for action to be taken at the level of the Croatian community. So on reading this I'm wondering this: Within the military HVO could it be that there were various and varying factions or trends? You were in the HVO; you had a command post or position in there. In your view were all the other officers in the same line, or did they have various thoughts about the Vance-Owen Plan, what was happening in Geneva? Was there differences of opinion which would explain why Mr. Lasic is trying to get everybody together again here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was signed by Commander Lasic, but in all armies like in the military district of Mostar, there was an organised department for political activity, and it is this officer that led this meeting. His rank was equal to mine. It was a regular political briefing on topics that cropped up at the moment. Why the commander of the 1st Brigade was absent, he probably had the same information from the press or any other media. This was widely discussed in the street and in family homes, because whatever agreement was proposed, we looked at it eagerly and hopefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are only partly answering my question. What I would like to know is this: All the military and officers within the HVO, were you all in favour of the Vance-Owen Plan or were some people not in agreement? You might have been among those people. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was never able to review the Vance-Owen Plan in detail. I knew about it only from briefings like this. It was up to my superiors and my colleagues to accept what was required of us. Decisions were mostly unanimous. There was no lack of discipline and nobody disagreed. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I don't know how it was interpreted, but the witness answered your question precisely, the question how the Vance-Owen Plan was accepted. He said, "We looked at it like it was a ray of sunshine." That means with joy, and let the witness deny this if I'm not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English translation does not quite coincide with what the witness has said. Did you say in your language what Mr. Praljak has just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we in Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially in Mostar, are fond of very picturesque language, but I will probably need to be more specific in my statements. Yes, this correction is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you used a metaphor to qualify the standpoint of the officers of the HVO. Mrs. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: At transcript page 48231, Judge Antonetti asked you: "If General Praljak had decided for some reason to destroy the Old Bridge, would he have -- would he have called the chief of artillery to see with him how best to go about it to destroy the Old Bridge?" And your answer was: "If that had been the plan, I'm sure that he would have called me. Either me or anybody else in that position. If it had been me, I would not have taken upon myself such a duty." Mr. Maric, why would you not have taken it upon yourself such a duty?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Old Bridge in Mostar was a part of every man and woman in Mostar. It was a part of me. And despite the fact that it was used many times as a military facility for crossings by the BH Army and for crossings by the HVO at the time when we were waging war against the JNA, I would have never allowed myself to do something like that. In fact, I would have tried to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, your good opinion of the bridge was shared by many Muslims and Croats alike; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear this very well. Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your good opinion of the bridge was shared by many Muslims and Croats alike?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: There is a typing noise when you listen to the translation, so probably somewhere the typing should be stopped. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, did you know other Croatian HVO soldiers who would also have been against destroying the bridge?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe will be a better answer if I say that I didn't know a single Croat, a single soldier who would want to destroy the Old Bridge. I did not know anyone who would wish to destroy the Old Bridge. That means that all the people I knew did not want it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that any decision or desire to destroy the bridge would have been controversial and unacceptable even to soldiers in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be controversial, unacceptable, and unfeasible within the circles of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you would agree that if it had been destroyed, the expectation would be that it would garner worldwide attention, which of course it did.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that the destruction of the Old Bridge, with good reason, garnered public attention in the whole world, as well as opprobrium, and I hope that in the near future truth will finally be established, the real truth will finally be established about the destruction of the Old Bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, if there had been a person who had ordered the destruction of the Old Bridge, do you agree with me that that person would be aware of the expected outrage that such an order would receive and would want to keep his identity unknown?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question. Could you perhaps put it in simpler terms.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes. It was probably a bad question. Would you agree with me that if a person had ordered the destruction of that bridge, they would know that that was an order they wanted to keep it quite? They wanted to keep it a secret. They didn't want everybody to know they were the one who did it.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the destruction of any building and especially a bridge, and particularly in a position where the Old Bridge was located, was such a tall order organisationally and in terms of execution, that it could never ever have been done by a small group or an individual. That could not have come down from a superior command. I reject the idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
