utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric. Let's look at an order, P06534. P06534. This is -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Mr. Maric, I'm still on the Old Bridge, because I'm currently working on it, and I'm going to put a question to you. The Trial Chamber is seized of several versions concerning the destruction of the Old Bridge. The Prosecutor has one version. The Defence of General Praljak has told us that it is likely that the Muslims blasted the bridge with explosives and a strong jet of water, and that is why the bridge collapsed, and on a video which I intended to show you, but we won't have time for that, we can she that shots have been fired from a tank, but we can also see that a project -- projectile comes from the other side, the other bank. So this is where it comes from. However, we also know that there were tank drivers inside the tanks. And if I remember correctly, there were three of them. It seems that one died and two remained. I was very surprised about the fact that the Prosecutor did not call those two tank drivers, those two survivors, to ask them who had given them an order to shoot at the bridge. Then we would have gone up the chain of command. That is very easy. That is how you conduct an investigation. It is as easy as pie. Perhaps we have never seen these tank drivers. We don't know what's become of them. We know that an investigation was carried out, and then everything just vanished into thin air, and nobody did anything about it. The only people seized of this issue is actually the Trial Chamber. You were a military in the HVO at the time, and I've put the question to you already, but you haven't quite answered the question. How is it then that the command of the HVO did not order an investigation, a detailed investigation, into this matter for the truth to rise to the surface? Because 16 years down the road, the truth has still not be revealed. How can you explain this? If you just with very a banal investigation process, lead it the way it should be led, we could have gone up the chain of command. We could have understood who gave the order. We would have seen the tank drivers who would have told us who had actually given the order. Why was this not done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know why this has not been done thoroughly and finalised. I know you are interested in the Old Bridge. The entire public is. But let me just say this: The position that is said to have been the origin of the projectiles is such that with all available means from the positions of the BH Army the bridge can easily be destroyed by the very first projectile. As an officer and as a human being, I could never be persuaded by anyone that the units on the left bank of the Neretva River could not have prevented it unless they have been -- unless they had been involved themselves. Thus with all assets available to the BH Army, that position could have been instantaneously neutralised. That is perfectly clear to anyone and everyone in Mostar, on the left bank and the right bank of the Neretva alike. That's why I said that we are still no closer to the truth. Let's not forget that the rulers of the town sold their property on the left bank and the right bank and went to live elsewhere. I went -- the rulers further to east and the ruling classes, and they did that the moment they realised their intentions had failed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a question of a technical nature. If, for instance, a cannon or a unit under your command opens fire and supposing the cannon had destroyed the Old Bridge, did you understand this is a working assumption, you're not involved. I'm just -- would you like me to repeat it? So I shall repeat. So let's imagine that an artillery unit, an artillery piece placed under your command opens fire, fires are shot and it destroys the Old Bridge. Then an investigation would have been conducted and the -- and the person who fired the artillery piece would be asked whether he had fired the shot. It's a firing officer who has asked us and told us to fire at this target. And would the officer then be asked, Who asked you to do this? And then he would have turned around and said, It was Colonel Maric. Is that how things would have happened? I'm talking in military terms, if such an investigation had been conducted by the military.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably. It would have had to be like that then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mrs. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Madam Usher, I believe the witness needs some help.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P06534. This is November 8th. This is an order for offensive combat operations. It's a packet order, so it's not signed. And it's from General Petkovic. Number 1, it says --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe my learned friend probably anticipated my objection because he -- she correctly said this concerns Paket radio, and it's not signed. We discussed this already during the testimony of General Praljak, and he said that on that day General Petkovic had not been in Citluk. It is recorded on 44461 page of the transcript and on other occasions as well. So this order can be -- cannot be considered as an order from General Petkovic regardless of the name on the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And just procedurally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: -- I certainly understand Mrs. Alaburic's concerns, but they're better placed in a question on redirect or in closing. So I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P06534. It says, Order, number 1: "HVO units on all sectors of the front must switch to offensive operations immediately." And then it says: "2. Focus the attacks on the following axis: Gornji Vakuf to Novi Travnik, Kiseljak to Busovaca. And then: "3. In the Mostar military district carry out offensive operations with smaller formations in the areas of Salakovac, Bijelo Polje, the town of Mostar, Blagaj. And then it says: "Shell the town of Mostar selectively at various intervals." Mr. Maric, in your experience in military -- well, in your experience, when orders were issued regarding offensive operations, did they normally include a specific targeting information? We've seen a couple.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Were you aware that the day before this order was issued on November 8th, the day before, November 7th, there was a meeting called in Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware, Your Honour. You'd have to remind me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We can go to 3D00793. This is the loose one, I think in the back or under the binder. 3D00793. This is dated November 7th. It's also on the screen. And this reflects conclusions from the meeting of the Main Staff --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me for being meticulous, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The document here is called 4D00793. Is this an error in the writing or in the speaking?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think there's both 3D and 4D. So I'm looking for 3D793. And, Your Honour, it's loose. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Got it. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It's conclusions from a meeting with the Main Staff and commanders of certain zones. And it says: "On the 7th of November, from 1800 hours and 1900 hours, a meeting of the commander of the Main Staff with the commanders of the districts of Tomislavgrad and Mostar, as well as individual troops, has been held." And then it goes into what was discussed. I'm not going to go into those issues. But I'm going to go to the second page where you have a number of people listed, and these are the people who are listed at this meeting. Sir, I know this was a long time ago, but I see your name, Vinko Maric. And above it I see Miljenko Lanic. I believe it's a typo. But does this help you remember whether you and General Lasic attended this meeting on the 7th?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was present at this meeting on the 7th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you have any memory of General Petkovic being there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm more inclined to believe that he was not. I can't recall exactly, but I don't think General Petkovic was there. Maybe somebody in this courtroom knows better.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Nonetheless, there are many people there, and I imagine there were all sorts of discussions. Is it possible that there were discussions to which you were not privy?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this meeting or generally?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: At that meeting.

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are elements here with which I personally was not familiar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm still on this document which has already been mentioned. At the time I put a question. I believe it was to General Praljak. And I see all these officers who address themselves to the president of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the parliament, to the government, to the Main Staff, and I was wondering whether this might be the signs of sedition inside the military HVO where some are not happy with what is happening and are asking people to address their problems. As by way of an example, look at item 6: "Establish a unique line of command, a one and only line of command." So I thought that if officers write this, it means that there must certainly have been parallel command lines. Otherwise, why would they have included this?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Replace Republic of Bosnia Herzegovina with HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It so happens that you attended this meeting. What did you wish to demonstrate with this kind of meeting? Because in other countries officers are sometimes unsatisfied, and this ends in a coup d'etat sometimes. And the government in place executes the rebellious officers. Was this a moment of dissatisfaction, and you turned to the politicians at the time? But my question is why did you organise such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I know for a fact this was not an attempt -- an attempt to impose military will on civilian authorities. I know that for sure. I also know that at this time, we were completely exhausted, materially and morally. We had suffered many aggressive attacks, and we felt spent in terms of materiel and human resources. And words of caution were probably called for from this level as well to take certain steps to raise the HVO to a level that would enable it to do its job properly in defending the lines and the territory. That is how I understand it. If it had been a really dramatic meeting, I would have remembered more details, which I can't. I remember that I spent the most time in this meeting with my colleagues from artillery with whom I met very rarely, and I believe I joined this group at my own request more in order to see them than to discuss the agenda of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is 12.30. We need to have our last break for this morning. We shall have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I know that -- I know that both today and tomorrow time is the concern, but nonetheless there's a matter that I think is sufficiently important, in the Prosecution's view, that needs to be raised before the end of this week. I was hoping - frankly, I think the witness that we're now on - might end a little bit earlier, and we'd have time today to deal with it. However since we're now in the last session, I felt that I had no real alternative but to raise the issue now because time tomorrow will be no less sensitive presumably than today, and I don't want the week to end, with all respect to the Chamber, without raising what for the Prosecution -- what the Prosecution believes is an important issue. Your Honours, the Court well knows that Rule 65 ter (G)(i)(b) requires that before the commencement of the Defence case, the Pre-trial Judge shall order the Defence to file a witness summary for each witness to be called including the points in the indictments as to which each witness will testify. In connection with the decision postponing the commence of the Defence cases on the 28th of January, 2008, the Trial Chamber delayed the commencement of the Defence cases from 17 March 2008 to 5 May 2008. In that decision the Trial Chamber stated at page 6 as one of the reasons for delaying the start of the Defence case is that it, quote, and I'm quoting: "Had to ensure that the right of the Prosecution to a fair trial is respected and that it has the possibility to prepare the cross-examination of defence witnesses." As part of the same 28 January decision, the Trial Chamber ordered the Defence to make all of their rule 65 ter (G) filings including witness summaries, quote, "at the latest by 31 March 2008." At page 7 of the Court's decision. I say again, quote, "at the latest." The various Defence teams, including the Petkovic Defence, made their 65 ter (G) filings on 31 March 2008. The Petkovic Defence ruling 65 ter (G) filing listed Milivoj Petkovic as Witness number 16. He was listed as a witness on the Petkovic Defence witness list. The Petkovic filing, however, concerning the witness Petkovic provided no summary and no other information except that his testimony would relate to "all counts." Again, contrary to Rule 65 ter (G), contrary to the Trial Chamber's 28 January 2008 order, the list provided no summary for Mr. Petkovic's testimony, provided no information as to which paragraphs in the indictment his evidence would address, provided no list of exhibits that would be used in connection with his testimony. Now, before continuing on, Your Honours, let me make the foundational Prosecution position clear. According to the rules and the Trial Chamber's own orders, the Prosecution should have received a fully adequate witness summary for Mr. Petkovic not later than 31 March 2008. By that measure and jumping ahead for a moment to the fact that we did finally receive a summary on the 11th of January, 2010, which I'll come back to momentarily, by that measure, Your Honours, that summary is more than a year and a half late. Now, continuing on the history more generally, the Prosecution submits that since the commencement of the defence cases in May 2008 and ever since then, I'm sure the Chamber knows and perhaps has grown weary at times of hearing it from us, but the Chamber knows the Prosecution's position on the timely receipt of fully adequate witness summaries. It's been addressed a number of times which we believe is fully consistent and required by Tribunal jurisprudence, rules, and practice. In one of its ongoing rulings on this topic, in fact, on the 22nd of January, 2009, the Trial Chamber said that it was not required that the Prosecution raise all of its objections to all possible summaries at one time, but that the appropriate procedure would be to raise them on a case-by-case basis. And that is what we have tried to do ever since. On the 24th of April, 2008, in its decision adopting guidelines for the presentation of Defence evidence, the Trial Chamber in guideline number 4, paragraph 3, provided that a party presenting its case must provide to the Trial Chamber and the parties, "a schedule of the witnesses it intends to call for one month." On the 2nd of October, 2008, the Trial Chamber issued a further decision on this topic in which it made it clear that as to the witness calendar that a party must file concerning all the witnesses, all the witnesses it will call for one month, this schedule, quote, "must be filed 30 days before the testimony of the first witness for the month to which the schedule refers." Now, by practice and by the Prosecution's understanding, that would mean, for example, that the trial calendar for -- for all of -- for the entire month of February was due to be provided to the Prosecution on the 1st of January, 30 days before the first witness to be called in February. Now, the Prosecution submits, Your Honours, that the practice that has evolved is the Prosecution following the above guidance has generally not raised issues about the adequacy of witness statements or witness summaries until the time when it -- when it first receives or receives the monthly calendar in advance of the first witness to be called in the following month. While the Prosecution -- while the Prosecution during the fall of 2009, in at least two letters, on 18 September and 16 November, raised the question of notice and a witness summary for Mr. Petkovic, it had no notice that Mr. Petkovic would -- would be called as a witness commencing on 1 February until it received for the first time the Petkovic Defence trial calendar for February on January 1. Throughout the past number of months, since at least our first letter on the 18th of September and a second letter on the 16th of November, the Prosecution understood that it would receive a fully adequate summary concerning Mr. Petkovic's testimony if not on 31 March 2008, when it was first required, but at least no less than 30 days before he would commence giving his testimony. In fact, Your Honours, separate and apart from anything else, the Prosecution understood that we had an agreement with the Petkovic Defence based on an exchange of correspondence on the 16th and 17th of November of 2009, that a fully adequate summary would be received by -- from the Petkovic Defence for each person giving testimony at least 30 days in advance at the same time that they provided the trial calendar that the Chamber requires. However, when we received -- when the Prosecution received the Petkovic calendar on -- for February, we did not receive a summary for Mr. Petkovic when he was listed to commence his testimony on the 1st of February. In our letter to the Petkovic Defence addressing this situation sent on the 4th of January, 2010, a week ago, we objected to the fact that we had not received a summary, and we asked once again to please receive one. We also gave notice that we opposed and would oppose the commencement of Mr. Petkovic's testimony until we had a fully adequate summary at least 30 days prior to the commencement of his testimony. Now, apparently the Petkovic Defence says that there was a misunderstanding and that they never agreed to provide a summary for Mr. Petkovic. We take a different view, Your Honour. The Chamber, if its minded to, can look at the correspondence at some point, but we certainly understood that was our agreement in addition to everything else. But be that as it may, even putting a -- whether there was an agreement or not to one side, it is the Prosecution position that it has been owed a fully adequate summary for Mr. Petkovic since 31 March 2008 and every day thereafter. Consistent with the provision of trial calendars and practice, we fully expected to receive such a summary at least a full 30 days before Mr. Petkovic would commence his testimony. In fact, as I mentioned a few moments ago, following our letter objecting to the situation, we did receive a summary for Mr. Petkovic this past Monday, on the 11th of January, 2010. Now, consistent with the rules and practice, Your Honours, we ask that Mr. Petkovic's testimony should not commence on 1st of February, but only at least 30 days after the Prosecution has had the fully adequate summary required by the rules according to the time schedule that the Chamber has applied in the past. By that, Your Honours, we submit that Mr. Petkovic's testimony should not commence until 11 February which is 30 days after we received the summary. That is our position. It is simply to apply the rules and practice that this Trial Chamber has applied for a long time and the rules of the Tribunal. The Prosecution should not be at a disadvantage by not having received that summary within the time agreed and provided and, in our respectful submission, required. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to state my views. Unfortunately, until a minute ago I didn't know that my learned friend Mr. Scott will raise this issue today. However, I'm ready to respond. I'll start with last things first. The Petkovic Defence does not object to the Prosecutor's request to be allowed additional time to prepare the cross-examination of General Petkovic. The general Defence, however, would like to express its surprise that after four years, the Prosecutor - and six years after the indictment was issued and ten years into the investigation in this case - needs additional time to cross-examine any of the accused in the proceedings. However, if my learned friends from the Prosecution deem that they still don't know the case sufficiently enough in order to carry out the cross-examination the way they wish, we absolutely do not object to additional time being accorded to them. I would like to provide several clarifications, because I believe that my learned friend Mr. Scott has misinformed you about the essence of our communication. As far as our possible agreement with the Prosecutor as to whether we will provide them with the summary or not, I would like to decline any possibility for anybody to believe that we had -- we have agreed on anything with the Prosecutor's office. We have informed the Prosecutor's office about our positions as to when we would do things, and we do what we think we should do in keeping with the rules of the Tribunal and the rules that have been established by the Trial Chamber. And this involves not only the Prosecutor's office but all the other Defence teams which are certainly interested -- as interested, if not even more interested, to know what General Petkovic will say during his testimony, because the other Defence teams also have the right to have enough time to prepare for cross -- cross-examination. Irrespective of any possible interpretations as to whether an accused has different rights and obligations with regard to any other witness, we did not have any doubts that we would indeed provide a summary of the facts that General Petkovic will testify about as is prescribed by the rules. I am looking at the transcript, and I would like to correct a few things. Not summary of the facts, but summary on the facts - [In English] Summary on the facts - [Interpretation] that the General will be talking about, but because this is prescribed by the rules of this Tribunal. As far as the practice of this Trial Chamber is concerned, we have relied on what happened during the General Praljak Defence case. If we calculated the time well, General Praljak provided his summary about 18 or 19 days prior to the beginning of his testimony. The Prosecutor's Office did not have any objection to that. We provided the summary of General Petkovic's testimony some 20 days prior to his expected testimony. The schedule for Mr. Petkovic's testimony has been provided to all the parties and the Trial Chamber in due time in keeping with the guidelines. All we are going to hear from General Petkovic during his testimony as regards topics and basic thesis is familiar to everybody in the courtroom from the 26th of October, 2009, when the Petkovic Defence outlaid the essential thesis of its Defence case in its opening statement. As far as the time accorded to the Prosecutor for cross-examination, we would like to say the fact that General Petkovic is going to testify has been known at least since 31st March 2008. In our 65 ter list, there is a list of documents that the Defence intends to use during Mr. Petkovic's testimony. In addition to those documents we also have the right to use all the other documents that are already in evidence. Therefore, the Prosecutor should not find it surprising. I would like to restate if my learned friends need additional time, I don't object because the General Petkovic team is looking forward to a good cross-examination, the part of the Prosecutor's team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to add a couple of words to my learned friend Alaburic's words. I don't want to embark on a discussion. This is the matter of the interested parties. I would like to support my learned friend Alaburic's words, save for one position where she says that General Petkovic's team is tolerant towards the Prosecutor's office and they do not object to additional time being given to them before the testimony of this witness starts. I object to that. I don't think that we have the luxury of any more delays in this courtroom. Very soon we will have spent four years in this courtroom. We all know what the reason for that is. Nobody could influence that, either us or the Trial Chamber. The situation is what it is. I'm just reminding you of an obvious fact, and that is that the accused are detained. My client has been detained for such a long time, and any delays, further delays, are out of the question because that would jeopardise the right of the accused to an expeditious trial, and this cannot be done for any banal reasons. If the Prosecutor has not grasped so far what General Petkovic might be testifying about, they should not have issued the indictment in the first place. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Ms. Alaburic, you told us that if the Prosecutor should need any additional time, you would not object to it. But would this mean that were General Petkovic to testify on the 11th of February, you would call other witnesses between the 1st and the 11th, so that there's no gap. Or does that mean that we have to stop until the 11th of February?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we designed our defence in such a way that Mr. Petkovic would be the last witness. We know we have more time at our disposal, but we thought we should leave some time aside in view of the position of the Trial Chamber that in case the need arises to examine the witnesses of other Defence teams for longer than the Petkovic Defence would normally have, we might use for that purpose our own time. And we estimated that in order to examine future witnesses, especially from the Defence of Praljak, we might well use our own time to cross-examine them. Since in view of the Trial Chamber this use of time would be considered as part of the Defence case, we would not use our time to examine Petkovic witnesses, but we saved this time for witnesses who might be speaking to the same events, the same localities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm at a loss, Ms. Alaburic, because I seem to understand that Mr. Petkovic would have 6 hours as of the 1st of February, and that you would have further witnesses. Now you're telling that Mr. Petkovic is going to be your last witness. In other words, we have Colonel Maric now, then we have tomorrow's witness. There's another one scheduled for two weeks. Then there would be General Petkovic, and that would be it. You have no further witnesses. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. I thought what I was saying would be abundantly clear, because we left the second half of February without any witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, if the Trial Chamber were to grant Mr. Scott's request, the testimony of General Petkovic would start on the 11th of February. So there would be no hearing for ten days. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to give the floor back to Mr. Scott, but let me say this, for Mr. Scott to understand fully what I meant to say, regardless of the Trial Chamber's view and decision: Firstly, the Security Council, on the 19th of December, issued a Resolution extending my own mandate until June 2010. So I don't know at all what is going to be my fate after June. If the trial were not to be concluded, finished, I should have another mandate extending the current one, but I have no clue about it. In this Resolution, which I'm going to quote in an opinion that I'm going to file today, it is said that the Security Council is asking for the proceedings to be sped up, and General Petkovic has testified in other proceedings, in two other proceedings. So what he may say is well known to the Prosecutor, and I'm somewhat surprised that the Prosecutor should need so much time to prepare for the cross-examination of General Petkovic. Thirdly, let me add this, this issue of the summaries: Personally, I think that an accused who testifies is not any ordinary witness. I believe that there's no need for a prior summary before an accused testifies. That's my take on the rules. An accused at a stretch can sit down and say, I'm innocent, you've heard me. Thank you very much, I'm going to go back to the dock. And that would be his testimony. There's no need for a summary. But if my fellow Judges were of a different view, it may be that Mr. Scott's request will be granted. This being said, what do you have to say, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I'll start at the end and work a bit backwards. I don't think the completion strategy should be used to the disadvantage of any party in the case, including the Prosecution. The current schedule, and whether there's down time in February, that is not of our making. That is not of our making, and it's not fair to lay any disadvantage at the foot of the Prosecution. We didn't make that schedule. It could have been -- we could have received the summary when we should have received it. That was not of our making. The schedule is not of our making. But what I hear the president saying is, is that, Well, if there's a problem now, it should work to the advantage of the Prosecution. I must respectfully disagree with that, Your Honours. And I will start with another smaller point. As to the timing of Mr. Praljak's summary, long story short, when Mr. Praljak began his testimony everyone in the courtroom knew that his direct examination would be going on for weeks, if not months. It's a completely different situation in terms of the time that the Prosecution had to prepare for his cross-examination. That direct examination went on for months. Of course during that time, the Prosecution had a chance to prepare its case. Not a six-hour direct, which Ms. Alaburic says is the time that she will use for Mr. Praljak. Completely, utterly different situation. There is no distinction, Your Honours, under Tribunal law between a witness and an accused for purposes applying Rule 65 ter. At least two Chambers have specifically ruled to that effect, Judge Moloto in the Martic case on 7 July 2006, quote: "If you, the Defence, are going to call Mr. Martic as a witness, then he is a witness. You must give a 65 ter summary for his testimony. If you're going to call Mr. Martic as a witness, by the time that you give the detailed summaries of the witnesses to the Prosecution, you must have a detailed summary of Mr. Martic's testimony." Judge Orie ruled the same way in the Galic case on the 22nd of January, 2003. "There is no support in Tribunal jurisprudence Rules or practice as the Rule 65 ter (G) for making any distinction between an accused and any other witness." When the witness -- when an accused takes that witness stand he becomes a witness. He becomes a witness, and he takes an oath. He has to tell the truth, and the procedural rules apply, and there's no Tribunal rule to the contrary. In fact, the only Tribunal law on the topic supports the Prosecution position. Now, Your Honour, the other thing, and you know, we hear this every time. Oh, the Prosecution, why don't they understand their own case? Well, that's not the point, Your Honour. We shouldn't have to come in here and justify the application of the rules. The rules are the rules. You're essentially -- the Chamber's essentially asking us to -- well, justify to us why we should apply the rules. The rules should be applied because they're the rules, not because the Prosecution has to come in here and beg and give some specific reason why the rules should be followed. The rules should be followed because they are the rules. Now, we're not required to guess at what Mr. -- what Ms. Alaburic might cover in her six hours. A six-hour testimony in this case from the accused, quite frankly, is a very limited amount of time. I submit to the Chamber that Ms. Alaburic is going to have to be very selective in the topics that she chooses to cover in six hours. The Chamber, Your Honours, are well aware of the usage of time in the courtroom and how much time it takes. She'll have -- she says she's going to use six hours. It's a small amount of time for an accused. Now the Prosecution in that context can't be left in the situation of simply guessing of what selective topics Ms. Alaburic is going to cover in that six hours. It could be hundreds of things. Well, we're going to talk about the whole case. Well, no they're not, because they can't talk about the whole case in six hours; it's impossible. She is going to have to be selective, and we have the right and should have the opportunity to be equally selective, if you will, in preparing to meet not just any imaginary testimony, not one of a hundred, 500 topics, but the very topics and the testimony that he proposes to give. We have a fundamental right, I submit to Your Honours, the victims in this case, the international community, and the Prosecution that represents those victims has the right to a fair trial too. And we have the right to an adequate preparation to meet not just any imaginary or fantasy testimony of Mr. Petkovic, but the actual testimony that he will give in this courtroom. And that requires, and Tribunal law requires, that we be provided a fully adequate summary. That should have been provided to us on 31 March 2008; we didn't get it. We've waited. We sent correspondence in the fall; we didn't get it. We thought we would get it at least 30 days in advance. Excuse me. Excuse me. I'm not going to compete with comments. We thought we would at least receive it within the 30 days, so we waited; we were patient. And then we received a calendar for the first time on January 31, which we appreciate, 30 days in advance of February, telling us for the first time that that's when Mr. Petkovic would in fact be called; fine. We didn't get our summary. We sent our letter to the effect saying, Where's the summary? We didn't receive it. Your Honour, that's just -- I don't need -- I don't think -- and with the greatest respect to all the Judges and the Chamber, I don't think the Prosecution should have to come up and justify why the rules should be applied. We should have gotten a summary. We should have adequate time to prepare. Ms. Alaburic says she doesn't object. Well, if she doesn't object; she doesn't object. And if there's issues about the scheduling, those are not of the Prosecution's making. Those are not of the Prosecution's making, and it shouldn't be -- that should not be laid at our feet. Now as to the schedule, Your Honours, if you notice -- if you look at the calendar for February, you will note that instead of, in fact, getting a full calendar for the full month, we, in fact, only have a calendar through the 16th of February. We should have received, the Trial Chamber should have received, the other co-accused should have received, we should have received, a calendar of all the witnesses for February. Instead, from 5th -- from the 17th of February on, for the next week and a half, all we have on the calendar is "spare/contingency." Week and a half. That's down time. That's downtime. Now, why should we disadvantaged because of that? Now the Chamber may want to ask what that time is going to be used for. And it also raises the question of when is the Coric going to begin? And when do we receive the list of the first Coric witnesses? We should have received that already, because we should have received a full calendar month schedule for February on the 1st of January. That means for the second half of February, we should have that schedule now. The Trial Chamber, the Judges, should have that schedule now. We have half a month calendar. Your Honour, none of these issues, none of those problems are issues of the Prosecution's making. We're in here, and we're trying to do our own -- the best job possible. Maybe no one cares much about the Prosecution, maybe the Prosecution doesn't get much sympathy. But we take our jobs as professionals. We're trying to do the best job we can for the Judges and present to the -- our positions and the evidence to the Chamber. The Chamber may ultimately disagree with our positions, but we're here trying to do a professional job. The rules should be applied because they are the rules, and we should get the time provided, and Ms. Alaburic has even told us she doesn't object. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I want your leave for a few words. I'll be very, very brief. I kindly ask you to allow me. I can't remember exactly at what moment this happened, but I think it might have been at the beginning of the testimony of General Praljak, and I remember this very clearly. I said several times in this courtroom that General Petkovic would be testifying, and I know for a fact that Honourable Judge Antonetti asked me how we planned to organise his testimony, whether it would be at the beginning of our case, and I said unequivocally at that time that it was our plan for General Petkovic to be our last Defence witness. At the time we presented our calendar for February, it was a fact that I considered completely beyond doubt. We planned that General Petkovic, according to our schedule, would be finished in the middle of February, and at that time I must confess I thought his testimony would last much longer because we expected questions from Judge Antonetti who questioned General Praljak for 22 hours, and we also expect that his questioning of General Petkovic might be not so long, but would still be long. And the testimony might thus extend to the end of February. But for purposes of scheduling, this is not something we could have planned exactly, because we don't know at this time for how long Judge Antonetti would be questioning General Petkovic. I would like to say something about certain words that are sometimes uttered by Mr. Scott in this courtroom in a tone that I believe is inappropriate and unprofessional. And the third thing I want to say is our commitment to the application of rules and principles. Claiming that he is committed to the application of rules, Mr. Scott actually told us that the Prosecutor in fact didn't care at all when General Praljak would hand in his summary because it was known in advance that his testimony would be long. But he does care when General Petkovic would hand in his summary because his testimony would be short. I perfectly understand the point Mr. Scott made, but what he said has nothing to do with the rules or the principles of this Tribunal. And in conclusion, let me respond to the position of Judge Antonetti concerning summaries. I just want to say that the accused, we believe, is entitled until the very end of this trial before this Tribunal, regardless of whose case it is, is entitled to say that he wants to testify, and the Trial Chamber would certainly not allow itself to refuse any of the accused this right just because they did not indicate it in time. And the accused in this right can in no way be the same as regular witnesses except in as far as their obligation to tell the truth is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... a moment. I shall give the floor to Mr. Coric's Defence counsel. If I don't agree entirely with Mr. Scott, I do agree, nonetheless, with the fact that we don't have the list of Mr. Coric's witnesses yet. On that point, he is perfectly right. Why do we not have this list? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, until now, it was the practice in the courtroom to provide the list of witnesses 30 days prior to the first witness's appearance. Even if General Petkovic finishes on the 16th of February, the deadline for me would be the 16th of January. I had an exchange of correspondence with Mr. Scott, and I indeed reckoned with General Petkovic's testimony lasting until the 1st of March, so I said that in view of the possibility of this change and in view of the possibility that we might have to begin on the 16th of February, I promised Mr. Scott that he would get our list of witnesses by the end of this week. That's one thing. Second, neither Mr. Scott nor anyone else in the courtroom should worry if General Petkovic finishes with his case on the 16th or any other date. We are ready to begin our case without any delay, without any break. And we are also ready, regardless of the fact that we have much less resources than the Prosecution to start cross-examining General Petkovic without any delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will deliberate on the matter, and we shall hand down a decision, which will most certainly be an oral decision. This will be next Monday because between then and the beginning of February or the 11th of February, we still have time. We shall deliberate and issue a decision on the points addressed by Mr. Scott. We shall bring the witness into the courtroom now. The Prosecution has 50 minutes left, so we shall not finish today, and the witness will come back tomorrow. The following witness will start in the course of tomorrow, and we shall see whether he will come back on Monday or on another day. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, as the witness is being brought in, and that's exactly the next issue that I wanted to raise. It's -- well, I say obvious. I suppose anything's always possible in a courtroom, but it's highly unlikely that we would finish the witness tomorrow given the entire circumstances. So I'm not sure what Ms. Alaburic is telling us what the future will be for this witness. I understood that he could not come back on Monday. There was some discussion earlier in the week that the Trial Chamber, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, inquired whether Ms. Alaburic might inquire that he could possibly stay over. I don't remember ever hearing an answer to that. It seems fairly obvious that we won't be able to finish the witness tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic, what did the witness tell you, that he could stay till Monday, or that he would need to come back?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had an answer to that question ready yesterday morning. I even communicated a message to your staff that I would like to express that, however it was not necessary. The witness who is supposed to appear tomorrow cannot stay on Monday. He is fully prepared to come at some other time but not in January. January is a reporting month for him. He has a lot of commitments. But he can be back in February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry to intervene on this point, but this raises the question whether it is worth having a little piece of testimony tomorrow of this witness, and then in an uncertain future, perhaps the end of February start again afresh. We have had cases where cross-examination followed quite a long time after direct or not at all, I think, if I'm not mistaken, in one case. And that is not a very -- very good organisation. Now, as it appears that there is some empty time anyhow, I -- I wonder whether it would not be a better idea to send the witness home now and then have him come back for a full examination and cross-examination in one piece, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I would like to propose a compromise. The witness who is supposed to appear tomorrow is a witness for both General Petkovic and General Praljak, but he is not a joint witness. For each of the Defence teams he's speaking about a totally different subjects. If we hear him tomorrow as Petkovic's Defence witness, in one hour of direct examination, an hour for cross-examination, and half an hour for each of the other Defence teams as has been planned, we can finish that part tomorrow. The next time the witness comes back as General Praljak's witness, can come with all the other witnesses who are on 92 bis list. I believe that this is a logical division that will be suitable to all. I've already spoken about that with my learned friend Mr. Kovacic, Mr. Praljak's counsel, and he is in agreement with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That said, the Prosecutor still has 50 minutes left, and there might be a redirect. So it might not be so certain that you can finish with this witness tomorrow. Since the Prosecutor will have an hour to cross-examine him on 92 bis issues, it might be preferable then for the Prosecutor to cross-examine the witness as part of the Praljak Defence. And then you can pick up from there. The Trial Chamber will see how this works out. Whatever the case may be, the witness is here, and that is the most important question. I apologise. We made you wait, but we had procedural matters to see to. This means that we will ask you to stay on until tomorrow. We thought that we would be able to finish today, but that is not possible. You will have to come back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: The President is talking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor has -- can you hear me all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying that you will be coming back tomorrow morning because we won't have finished with your testimony. We have ten minutes left for today, and the Prosecutor has 50 minutes left to put questions to you. So you will be coming back tomorrow morning. I hope this is not a problem for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's only tomorrow, then it won't be a problem as regards my health. And I'm here to tell the truth, not to pose any conditions as to how long my testimony's going to last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have now ten minutes left. I shall give the floor to Mrs. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I proceed? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Maric, while you were gone, we actually tabbed your binder. And the document I'm going to talk about right now is the one right in front of you, which is P06524. This is a document dated November 8th. When we left off before the break, you had seen the Paket order from Petkovic on November 8th, and you talked about the meeting of the Main Staff in the Mostar district and Tomislav district on November 7th. So this is another order from November 8th, and this is Lasic order, and it says: "Pursuant to the order number," and it lists a number. "1. In all parts of the Mostar military districts theatre, all units must plan to launch offensive operations without delay. "2. Plan offensive operations with small units in the following areas: Salakovac, Bijelo Polje, City of Mostar, and Blagaj." And then it says: "Shell the city of Mostar selectively at different time intervals." Mr. Maric, that language is familiar to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Because it appears that Lasic just took the Petkovic order and forwarded it down the chain of command; correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And whether this order specifically articulated targeting the bridge or not, isn't that exactly what happened on November 8th, sir?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see a reference to the bridge as a target.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, that's exactly right. You don't see specific language as -- of the bridge as a target, but isn't it a fact, yes or no, that on November 8th, the Old Bridge was targeted by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under item 2 it says selectively shelling. At that moment the HVO knew about military targets and their nature, and that referred exclusively to those military targets which under the war doctrine served for the purpose of military units. They were used for the planning and the conduct of combat activities and operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maric. This order is timed at 1700 hours, and I want to go forward a bit more in the evening to P09993. You should see that tabbed right in front of you. This is a report from the same day from Lasic. Do you see that, P09993? And this is just two hours later. And in this report, under number 2.1, second paragraph, he writes: "We fired 122-millimetre mortars on the Razvitak building at 900 hours, and at 1000 hours we fired two 88-millimetre -- apologies are you receiving that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not been receiving any interpretation. I'm sorry. I didn't have any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Are you getting any interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. So under 2.1, second paragraph: "We fired two 120-millimetre mortar shells on the Razvitak building at 900 hours. And at 1000 hours, we fired two 88-millimetre shells on Sipad and Fejiceva Street. We fired two 120-millimetre MB shells on Muslim positions at the Bulevar between 1000 hours and 1015. And around 1430 we fired two projectiles from a 120-millimetre gun on the Bulevar just opposite to the health centre when at least three enemy soldiers were killed. We fired six 82-millimetre MB shells on the northern camp in Zalik during the day." And then the next sentence is: "From 8.10 in the morning our tank was opening fire from Stotina during the whole day, and it fired 50 projectiles on the Old Town. Our MB also fired two projectiles on Stari Grad around 1400 hours, and our PZS from Hum was opening fire at the south exit from the town today. So my first question, Mr. Maric, is on November 8th, would you agree that there is an HVO tank on Stotina firing on the Old Town? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tanks were not under my authority, so I wouldn't know whether there was one or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, sir, you testified earlier in this case that you had to have an understanding of the full HVO military operations in the town of Mostar to do your job. So would you agree with me that your knowledge of that tank was something you should have known?

utterances.speaker: VINKO MARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, neither then nor now did I have any ambition to know all the details. My attention focused on artillery, and in that part I was concerned with any serious activities such as the ones described in here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We can go to P09992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would only like to ask a clarification from the witness. If the 120-millimetre gun or guns had been under your command or under the command of other units of the HVO? It is my first question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was a 120-millimetre mortar. It was not a cannon. It's a different piece with different technical and tactical characteristics. It was under the command of the brigade commander that held the front line in his area of responsibility. What I'm saying is that he was in direct command of that piece.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to adjourn. It's quarter to 2.00. There is another hearing in the afternoon. Let us reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 14th day of January, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 25
